910.name: Prehistoric & Early Slavic Poland
910.description: The Lusatian culture, Biskupin fortified settlement, and the migration of West Slavic Lechitic tribes into the Vistula and Oder basins laid the foundations for the future Polish state.

sub_clusters.name: Lusatian Culture & Biskupin
sub_clusters.description: The Lusatian culture (1300–500 BCE) produced the remarkable fortified settlement of Biskupin. Celtic and Germanic influences in the Vistula region during the pre-Roman Iron Age.

sub_clusters.name: Roman-Era Contacts & Slavic Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The amber trade routes connecting the Baltic to Rome, Germanic tribal movements, and the gradual settlement of West Slavic Lechitic tribes (Polans, Vistulans, Masovians, Pomeranians) forming the ethnic foundation of Poland.

920.name: Piast Dynasty & Christianisation
920.description: Mieszko I's Baptism of Poland (966) established the Polish state and integrated it into Western Christendom. Bolesław I the Brave became the first king (1025). The Congress of Gniezno (1000) with Emperor Otto III cemented Poland's European status.

sub_clusters.name: Mieszko I & Baptism of Poland
sub_clusters.description: Mieszko I unified the Polanie and neighbouring tribes, adopted Christianity through the Baptism of Poland (966), and established the Gniezno diocese. His Dagome iudex document placed Poland under papal protection.
key_events: Baptism of Poland (966) — Mieszko I adopts Christianity

sub_clusters.name: Bolesław the Brave & Early Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: Bolesław I the Brave's Congress of Gniezno (1000), royal coronation (1025), and territorial expansion. Casimir I the Restorer's reunification, and the Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth (1138) dividing Poland into duchies.

920.name: Fragmentation & Reunification
920.description: Poland fragmented into rival duchies for nearly 200 years. Mongol invasions (1241) devastated the country. Władysław I the Elbow-high reunified Poland (1320), and Casimir III the Great (r. 1333–1370) created a powerful, prosperous kingdom.

sub_clusters.name: Ducal Fragmentation & Mongol Invasions
sub_clusters.description: Poland's division into rival Piast duchies, the catastrophic Mongol invasion (Battle of Legnica, 1241), German colonisation and urban growth (Magdeburg Law), and the gradual movement toward reunification.

sub_clusters.name: Casimir III the Great & Kingdom's Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Władysław I reunified the kingdom (1320). Casimir the Great (r. 1333–1370) founded the University of Kraków (1364), codified law (Statutes of Wiślica), and welcomed Jewish refugees with the Statute of Kalisz, famously 'finding a Poland of wood and leaving one of stone'.

930.name: Jagiellonian Dynasty & Golden Age
930.description: The Union of Krewo (1385) and marriage of Jadwiga to Jogaila created the Polish-Lithuanian personal union, the largest political entity in Europe. The Jagiellonian era brought the victory at Grunwald (1410), the Renaissance, and Copernicus.

sub_clusters.name: Union with Lithuania & Battle of Grunwald
sub_clusters.description: The Union of Krewo (1385), Christianisation of Lithuania, and the Battle of Grunwald (July 15, 1410) — the largest medieval European battle — where the combined Polish-Lithuanian forces defeated the Teutonic Knights. The Peace of Toruń (1466) recovered Pomerania.
key_events: Battle of Grunwald (July 15, 1410) — Teutonic Knights defeated

sub_clusters.name: Polish Renaissance & Copernicus
sub_clusters.description: The Jagiellonian golden age: Nicolaus Copernicus's heliocentric theory (De revolutionibus, 1543), the flourishing of Kraków as a cultural centre, religious tolerance, and the Execution of the Laws movement strengthening noble democracy.

930.name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
930.description: The Union of Lublin (1569) created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth — at its peak the largest European state. The unique 'Noble Republic' with elected kings, the Sejm, and liberum veto experienced gradual decline, ending in the three partitions that erased Poland from the map.

sub_clusters.name: Union of Lublin & Golden Liberty
sub_clusters.description: The Union of Lublin (1569), the election of Henry of Valois (1573) and the Henrician Articles establishing noble privileges, the Warsaw Confederation guaranteeing religious freedom (1573), and the expansion under Stefan Batory and Sigismund III Vasa.

sub_clusters.name: The Deluge & Commonwealth Decline
sub_clusters.description: The Khmelnytsky Uprising (1648), the catastrophic Swedish Deluge (1655–60) that devastated the country, the siege of Jasna Góra (1655), King Jan III Sobieski's relief of Vienna (1683), and the deepening dysfunction of the liberum veto.
key_events: Jan III Sobieski's relief of the Siege of Vienna (September 12, 1683)

sub_clusters.name: Partitions of Poland
sub_clusters.description: Saxon kings, Russian interference, the Bar Confederation (1768), the Constitution of May 3, 1791 (Europe's first modern constitution), the Kościuszko Uprising (1794), and the three partitions (1772, 1793, 1795) that erased Poland from the map of Europe.
key_events: Constitution of May 3, 1791 — first modern European constitution
Third Partition (1795) — Poland ceases to exist

940.name: Partitioned Poland & National Uprisings
940.description: Poland disappeared from the map for 123 years, divided between Russia, Prussia, and Austria. Repeated uprisings (1794, 1830, 1848, 1863) failed but preserved national consciousness. Polish culture flourished in exile and under oppression.

sub_clusters.name: Napoleonic Era & Duchy of Warsaw
sub_clusters.description: Polish Legions fighting alongside Napoleon, the creation of the Duchy of Warsaw (1807–1815), the brief hope of Polish restoration, and the Congress of Vienna's creation of Congress Poland under Russian control.

sub_clusters.name: November & January Uprisings
sub_clusters.description: The November Uprising (1830–31) against Russia and its brutal suppression, the Great Emigration (Chopin, Mickiewicz), the January Uprising (1863–64) and its aftermath of severe Russification, and the different conditions in Austrian Galicia vs. Russian and Prussian partitions.

sub_clusters.name: Positivism & Pre-Independence Movements
sub_clusters.description: Organic work and positivist nation-building, Henryk Sienkiewicz's Nobel Prize (1905), the emergence of competing political movements (Piłsudski's socialism, Dmowski's nationalism), and the alignment of WWI powers that made Polish independence possible.

950.name: Second Republic & World War II
950.description: The restored Polish Republic (1918) under Piłsudski survived the Polish-Soviet War (1920, 'Miracle on the Vistula') but fell to the joint German-Soviet invasion (September 1939). WWII brought unparalleled devastation: 6 million Polish citizens killed, the Holocaust, and the destruction of Warsaw.

sub_clusters.name: Independence & Polish-Soviet War
sub_clusters.description: Poland's reconstitution (November 11, 1918), Piłsudski as Chief of State, the Polish-Soviet War and the decisive Battle of Warsaw (August 1920, 'Miracle on the Vistula'), the Treaty of Riga (1921) establishing eastern borders, and Piłsudski's May Coup (1926).
key_events: Battle of Warsaw — 'Miracle on the Vistula' (August 1920)

sub_clusters.name: September Campaign & German-Soviet Occupation
sub_clusters.description: The joint German-Soviet invasion (September 1–17, 1939), the division of Poland under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Katyn massacre (April–May 1940) of 22,000 Polish officers by Soviet forces, Auschwitz-Birkenau as the epicentre of the Holocaust, and the systematic destruction of Polish intelligentsia.
key_events: German invasion of Poland — WWII begins (September 1, 1939)

sub_clusters.name: Warsaw Uprising & Liberation
sub_clusters.description: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (April–May 1943), the Warsaw Uprising (August–October 1944) — 63 days of heroic resistance while the Red Army watched from the Vistula's east bank — and the deliberate Nazi destruction of 85% of Warsaw. Soviet 'liberation' imposed a new political order.

950.name: Communist Poland & Solidarity
950.description: Soviet-imposed communist rule, territorial shifts westward, the Poznań protests (1956), repeated crises (1968, 1970, 1976), and the emergence of the Solidarity movement under Lech Wałęsa — the first independent trade union in the Eastern Bloc — that catalysed the end of communism in Europe.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinist Era & 1956 Thaw
sub_clusters.description: Territorial shifts (loss of eastern Kresy, gain of western Recovered Territories), communist consolidation, Stalinist repression, the Poznań June protests (1956), Gomułka's 'Polish October' thaw, and reconstruction of Warsaw.

sub_clusters.name: Crises & Solidarity Movement
sub_clusters.description: The March 1968 antisemitic purges, the December 1970 Baltic coast massacres, the election of Pope John Paul II (1978), the Solidarity movement born in the Gdańsk shipyard (August 1980), martial law under General Jaruzelski (December 13, 1981), and the Round Table negotiations (1989).
key_events: Solidarity trade union founded in Gdańsk (August 1980)

960.name: Democratic Transition & EU Poland
960.description: The Round Table Agreement (1989) and first semi-free elections catalysed the fall of communism across Eastern Europe. Poland's 'shock therapy' economic transformation, NATO (1999) and EU (2004) accession, and contemporary political polarisation under PiS.

sub_clusters.name: Transition & Shock Therapy
sub_clusters.description: The Round Table Agreement, Mazowiecki government, Balcerowicz's 'shock therapy' economic reforms, rapid privatisation, NATO membership (1999), and EU accession negotiations.

sub_clusters.name: EU Era & PiS Government
sub_clusters.description: EU accession (May 1, 2004), rapid economic growth ('Green Island' during 2008 crisis), the Smoleńsk air disaster (2010), PiS government (2015–2023) and rule-of-law disputes with the EU, Poland's role as a frontline state supporting Ukraine after 2022, and the 2023 return of pro-EU coalition government.
